# Linear response and the meaning of transport {#sec-linear-response}

A density profile broadens after a quench. A current flows between two reservoirs.
An equilibrium current autocorrelation decays. Under suitable limits these are
three measurements of the same transport coefficient, but they are not
interchangeable at arbitrary bias, time, or system size. This chapter derives
their relation and explains what a ballistic contribution means.

We assume undergraduate quantum mechanics and thermal density matrices. Units
are $\hbar=k_B=1$, and spin operators mean $S^a=\sigma^a/2$. A *susceptibility*
is a change in an observable per weak applied field. *Linear response* keeps
only the first power of that field. All equilibrium averages below are connected
when the observable has a nonzero mean.

## Deriving the retarded response

Start with $\rho_0=e^{-\beta H_0}/Z$ and perturb
$H(t)=H_0-f(t)B$. In the interaction picture, $B_I(t)=e^{iH_0t}Be^{-iH_0t}$
and the density matrix satisfies

$$
\dot\rho_I=-i[-f(t)B_I(t),\rho_I].
$$

To first order, replace $\rho_I$ inside the right side by $\rho_0$ and integrate
from the remote past:
$\delta\rho_I(t)=i\int_{-\infty}^tdt' f(t')[B_I(t'),\rho_0]$.
Taking a trace with $A_I(t)$, and using cyclicity, gives

$$
\delta\langle A(t)\rangle
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt'\,\chi_{AB}(t-t')f(t'),
\qquad
\chi_{AB}(t)=i\theta(t)\langle[A(t),B(0)]\rangle_0.
$$ {#eq-response-kubo}

The step function enforces causality: a later perturbation cannot affect an
earlier measurement. Our sign follows the explicit coupling **$-fB$**.
A convention using $+fB$ and $-i\theta[A,B]$ describes the same physics with
the conjugate field reversed. Reporting the coupling prevents a common sign
ambiguity.

Causality makes $\chi(\omega)=\int dt\,e^{i\omega t}\chi(t)$ analytic for
$\operatorname{Im}\omega>0$. Its real and imaginary parts are consequently
related by dispersion relations. With this convention $\chi''_{AA}(\omega)$
is nonnegative for $\omega>0$ in a passive thermal state: absorption requires
positive energy. “Passive” means that a cyclic weak drive cannot extract net
work from equilibrium.

A forced harmonic oscillator supplies a direct sign check. For
$H_0=p^2/(2m)+m\omega_0^2x^2/2$ and perturbation $-f(t)x$,
$x(t)=x\cos\omega_0t+p\sin\omega_0t/(m\omega_0)$.
Using $[x,p]=i$ gives
$[x(t),x]=-i\sin(\omega_0t)/(m\omega_0)$, hence
$\chi_{xx}(t)=\theta(t)\sin(\omega_0t)/(m\omega_0)$.
Its retarded Fourier transform is
$[m(\omega_0^2-(\omega+i0^+)^2)]^{-1}$.
At zero frequency the displacement is $\delta x=f/(m\omega_0^2)$, in the
same direction as the force. This check catches an inconsistent response sign
without relying on a remembered convention. The poles lie just below the real
axis and the positive-frequency absorption weight is positive, checking
causality and passivity simultaneously.

## Spectral representation and fluctuation–dissipation

Let $H_0|n\rangle=E_n|n\rangle$ and $p_n=e^{-\beta E_n}/Z$. Insert complete
energy eigenstates into the commutator. The two orderings differ by exchanging
$n$ and $m$; their coefficient becomes $p_n-p_m$. The regulated time integral
then gives

$$
\chi_{AB}(\omega)=\sum_{nm}
\frac{(p_n-p_m)A_{nm}B_{mn}}
{E_m-E_n-\omega-i0^+}.
$$ {#eq-response-lehmann}

The infinitesimal selects the retarded boundary condition. For $A=B=A^\dagger$,
using $\operatorname{Im}(x-i0^+)^{-1}=\pi\delta(x)$ yields

$$
\chi''_{AA}(\omega)=\pi\sum_{nm}(p_n-p_m)|A_{nm}|^2
\delta[\omega-(E_m-E_n)].
$$

Define the unsymmetrized fluctuation spectrum
$S_{AA}(\omega)=\int dt\,e^{i\omega t}\langle A(t)A(0)\rangle_c$.
Its spectral weight is $2\pi p_n|A_{nm}|^2$ at positive energy transfer
$\omega=E_m-E_n$. On that delta function,
$p_m=e^{-\beta\omega}p_n$, so

$$
\chi''_{AA}(\omega)=\frac{1-e^{-\beta\omega}}{2}S_{AA}(\omega).
$$ {#eq-response-fdt}

For the symmetrized spectrum
$S^{\mathrm{sym}}=[S(\omega)+S(-\omega)]/2$, this is
$S^{\mathrm{sym}}=\coth(\beta\omega/2)\chi''$.
At small $\beta\omega$, fluctuations are approximately classical and
$S^{\mathrm{sym}}\simeq2T\chi''/\omega$. At larger frequency the distinction
between absorbing and emitting energy is essential. The equilibrium relation
cannot be imposed on an arbitrary driven steady state merely because its
correlations look smooth. The foundational response construction is due to
@kubo1957response.

For numerical work, a finite system has a discrete spectral measure. Replacing
delta functions by Lorentzians of width $\eta$ produces a plot, not a new
physical scattering mechanism. A meaningful dc extrapolation must vary $L$ and
$\eta$ together, respecting the finite-size level and transport scales.

## Diffusive response and the Einstein relation

Let $n$ be a conserved density coupled to chemical potential $\mu$. Write
$\chi_\mu=\partial n/\partial\mu$. A local equilibrium density shift is
$\delta n_{\mathrm{eq}}=\chi_\mu\delta\mu$.
The current must vanish if the actual profile equals that equilibrium profile,
which fixes the linear constitutive relation

$$
j=-D\partial_x\delta n+D\chi_\mu\partial_x\delta\mu.
$$

Combining it with continuity and Fourier transforming in space and time gives

$$
\chi_{nn}(k,\omega)=\chi_\mu\frac{Dk^2}{Dk^2-i\omega}.
$$ {#eq-response-diffusive-pole}

The denominator is the *diffusion pole*: a mode with wave number $k$ relaxes at
rate $Dk^2$. The numerator enforces conservation. At $k=0$, a time-dependent
uniform potential cannot change the total charge in a closed system. Taking
$\omega\to0$ first at nonzero $k$ gives the thermodynamic susceptibility;
taking $k\to0$ first gives zero. These limits differ for a physical reason.

Define the generalized force $F=-\partial_x\mu$ for transport between locally
prepared reservoirs, and write $j=\sigma_{\mathrm{dc}}F$.
The resulting Einstein relation is

$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{dc}}=D\chi_\mu.
$$ {#eq-response-einstein}

The earlier external field in the diffusion equation enters with the opposite
sign to an internally prepared chemical-potential gradient; the static external
potential cancels the gradient rather than creating a current. Distinguishing
these setups removes another apparent sign paradox.

If a dimensionless field $\lambda=\beta\mu$ is used instead, its susceptibility
is $\chi_\lambda=T\chi_\mu$. At infinite temperature,
$\chi_\mu\to0$ while $\chi_\lambda$ stays finite. Papers often report the
reduced conductivity $T\sigma$, or normalize the current with $\lambda$.
Always check these conventions before comparing diffusion constants.

## Current correlations and ballistic weight

For a lattice with total current $J=\sum_xj_x$, the dissipative conductivity at
nonzero frequency can be written

$$
\operatorname{Re}\sigma(\omega)
=\frac{1-e^{-\beta\omega}}{2\omega L}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\,e^{i\omega t}\langle J(t)J(0)\rangle.
$$ {#eq-response-conductivity}

For electromagnetic response, a lattice vector-potential derivation must also
include the diamagnetic contact term; treating a density-gradient protocol is
a convenient way to isolate dissipative transport without hiding that issue.
Zero-frequency singularities require careful limiting definitions.

Use the convention

$$
\operatorname{Re}\sigma(\omega)
=2\pi\mathcal D\,\delta(\omega)+\sigma_{\mathrm{reg}}(\omega).
$$ {#eq-response-drude}

The *Drude weight* $\mathcal D$ measures a persistent current component. If the
thermodynamic equilibrium current correlation tends to a constant $C_\infty$,
then, under the corresponding bulk limits,
$\mathcal D=\beta C_\infty/(2L)$. The factor two belongs to the chosen
$2\pi\mathcal D$ convention. A nonzero Drude weight is ballistic transport.
A vanishing Drude weight does not establish diffusion: superdiffusion,
subdiffusion, or insulating behavior are also possible.

When the current correlation is integrable and the Drude term vanishes,
the dc Green–Kubo relation is

$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{dc}}=\frac{\beta}{L}
\int_0^\infty dt\,\operatorname{Re}\langle J(t)J(0)\rangle.
$$ {#eq-response-green-kubo}

The thermodynamic limit must precede recurrence-sensitive long times. Combining
with @eq-response-einstein relates the integrated equilibrium current correlation
to density spreading. If the integral grows with its upper cutoff, a finite
constant $D$ is not yet justified.

## A projection derivation of the Mazur bound

Why can an interacting system retain current? Part of the current may overlap
with operators that cannot evolve. This becomes a geometric statement in
operator space. Define the positive Kubo–Mori inner product

$$
(A,B)_\beta=\frac1\beta\int_0^\beta d\tau\,
\langle A^\dagger(-i\tau)B\rangle_c.
$$ {#eq-response-inner-product}

At infinite temperature it reduces to the normalized Hilbert–Schmidt product
$\operatorname{Tr}(A^\dagger B)/\dim\mathcal H$ after subtracting means.
Let $Q_a$ be conserved, centered operators. Their Gram matrix is
$C_{ab}=(Q_a,Q_b)_\beta$. If they are linearly independent, $C$ is invertible.
The orthogonal projection of the current is

$$
J_\parallel=\sum_{ab}Q_a(C^{-1})_{ab}(Q_b,J)_\beta,
\qquad J=J_\parallel+J_\perp.
$$

Because $J_\parallel$ is conserved and the two parts are orthogonal,
the time-averaged current autocorrelation is at least
$(J_\parallel,J_\parallel)_\beta$. The remaining time-averaged norm is
nonnegative, as seen by resolving energy differences. Therefore

$$
\mathcal D\geq\frac{\beta}{2L}
\sum_{ab}(J,Q_a)_\beta(C^{-1})_{ab}(Q_b,J)_\beta.
$$ {#eq-response-mazur}

This is a Mazur bound [@mazur1969bound]. It is a lower bound, not generally an
equality for an incomplete charge set. A zero bound says that the chosen
charges miss a persistent component or that none exists; it does not choose
between those alternatives. Symmetry can force overlaps to vanish even in an
integrable system. Quasilocal charges, whose density norms decay with spatial
support, can supply overlaps missed by familiar short-range charges.

## Worked example: the free XX chain

Under Jordan–Wigner transformation, the XX chain becomes free fermions with
hopping $J/2$ and dispersion $\epsilon(k)=J\cos k$. Its group velocity is
$v(k)=\partial_k\epsilon=-J\sin k$. The conserved occupation numbers are
$n_k=c_k^\dagger c_k$, and the total particle-number current is
$J_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_kv(k)n_k$. In the convention $S^z=1/2-n$, the
spin current is its negative. Their autocorrelations and Drude weights are
identical. Both currents commute with the Hamiltonian.
Thus the entire current is persistent.

At infinite temperature and half filling,
$\langle\delta n_k\delta n_q\rangle=\delta_{kq}/4$. In the large-$L$ limit,

$$
\frac{\langle J_{\mathrm{tot}}^2\rangle}{L}
=\frac14\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{dk}{2\pi}J^2\sin^2k
=\frac{J^2}{8},\qquad
\lim_{T\to\infty}T\mathcal D=\frac{J^2}{16}.
$$ {#eq-response-xx-drude}

There is no finite diffusive coefficient in this ideal isolated model. Adding
weak dephasing changes the problem: momentum occupations relax and a finite
conductivity may emerge. The order of weak-scattering and long-time limits
then matters.

## How to compare three transport protocols

For equilibrium dynamics, compute $C(x,t)$ or the current integral. For a weak
step in $\lambda$, linear response relates the ensuing profile to equilibrium
correlations. The bias must be small enough that changing it rescales the signal
without changing its normalized shape. For a boundary-driven chain, solve a
master equation and measure the steady current versus size. A diffusive bulk
with fixed small density difference gives $j\propto L^{-1}$ after contact
resistances are negligible; a ballistic bulk can give a size-independent current.

A finite bias can prepare states far from the equilibrium sector of interest.
The strongly driven exact XXZ NESS in @prosen2011ness illustrates why its
size dependence must not be substituted automatically for the infinite-temperature
linear-response exponent. The exactly solvable dephased XX model in
@znidaric2011dephasing instead provides a valuable controlled laboratory for
boundary gradients and bulk scattering. A master equation also has its own bath
model assumptions; thermodynamic consistency should be checked when reservoirs
are interpreted as thermal baths.

A minimal Julia consistency check builds $H$ and $J$ in one magnetization
sector, diagonalizes $H$, and compares the spectral sum in
@eq-response-conductivity with direct $\operatorname{Tr}[J(t)J]/\dim\mathcal H$.
First verify Hermiticity, $[H,Q]=0$, and the local continuity identity. Compare
sectors carefully: fixed-charge ensembles suppress global charge fluctuations
but can approach grand-canonical local results in a suitable thermodynamic limit.

## Nearly conserved currents and the singular weak-scattering limit

A transparent interpolation between ballistic and diffusive response is a
current that is exactly conserved at $g=0$ but decays slowly for $g\neq0$.
Suppose, over a controlled window, its equilibrium autocorrelation is
$\langle J(t)J(0)\rangle/L=Ae^{-\gamma|t|}$.
Substitution into the high-temperature current formula gives

$$
\operatorname{Re}\sigma(\omega)
=\beta A\frac{\gamma}{\gamma^2+\omega^2},\qquad
\sigma_{\mathrm{dc}}=\frac{\beta A}{\gamma}.
$$ {#eq-response-broadened-drude}

The integrated spectral weight is $\pi\beta A$, independent of $\gamma$.
As $\gamma\to0^+$, the Lorentzian tends to $\pi\beta A\delta(\omega)$,
recovering the convention $\mathcal D=\beta A/2$. At any fixed nonzero
$\gamma$, the strict long-time current vanishes; at times short compared with
$\gamma^{-1}$, it appears persistent. This example makes the noncommuting
weak-scattering and long-time limits explicit.

A *memory matrix* approach generalizes this idea by projecting onto several
nearly conserved operators. Their equilibrium overlaps provide the static
matrix, while correlations of their weak time derivatives determine relaxation
kernels. Replacing those kernels by constants is a Markov approximation and
produces a matrix of decay rates. One should include all comparably slow
operators: eliminating an almost conserved mode can make the remaining memory
strongly frequency dependent. The single exponential above is a useful benchmark,
not an automatic form for weakly nonintegrable spin chains.

A simple check uses the driven hydrodynamic equation for a uniform current,
$\dot j+\gamma j=\mathcal W F(t)$, with response weight
$\mathcal W=\beta A$. A sinusoidal force gives
$\sigma(\omega)=\mathcal W/(\gamma-i\omega)$. Its real part reproduces
@eq-response-broadened-drude, while its imaginary part is odd in frequency.
The pole lies at $\omega=-i\gamma$, in the lower half-plane as required by
causality. A numerically fitted response with the pole in the upper half-plane
would describe an instability or a sign error, not passive relaxation.

The same crossover appears in a density packet. For times much shorter than
the scattering time, quasiparticles propagate approximately ballistically. At
later times, repeated direction randomization can yield diffusion with
$D\sim v^2/\gamma$, up to dimensional and angular factors. This kinetic estimate
must not be mistaken for a rigorous coefficient in a strongly correlated system.
It explains why both long observation times and long systems are needed near
integrability: the mean free path grows as the scattering rate shrinks. A chain
shorter than that mean free path can look ballistic even when its eventual bulk
transport is diffusive.

## Research bridges and open questions

@prosen2011drude showed that boundary-driven matrix product constructions can
reveal pseudolocal conservation laws and rigorous high-temperature lower bounds
on ballistic XXZ transport. The methodological lesson is that a dissipative
calculation can discover structure in a closed Hamiltonian. Reproduce the
projection inequality first with numerically known conserved operators; only
then attempt the infinite auxiliary-space construction.

The broad review @bertini2021transport connects exact charges, numerical
methods, and experimentally relevant chains. It is a map for deciding which
observable and limit a paper actually establishes. Near integrability, the
relaxation of nearly conserved charges introduces long crossovers; the 2026
preprint @santra2026crossover studies that crossover within a relaxation-time
collision model. Its transport coefficients are predictions of that collision
approximation, not universal microscopic coefficients for every perturbation.
Deriving controlled collision kernels and their slowest eigenmodes remains a
concrete route from integrable transport to ordinary hydrodynamics.

## Exercises and selected solutions

1. Starting from $H'=-fB$, derive @eq-response-kubo and track its sign. Repeat
   for a harmonic oscillator forced by $-f x$ and check the static response.
2. Derive detailed balance $S(-\omega)=e^{-\beta\omega}S(\omega)$ and show that
   @eq-response-fdt implies positive absorbed power at positive frequency.
3. Derive the Mazur bound for two nonorthogonal conserved charges. Show that
   changing their basis by an invertible matrix leaves the bound unchanged.
4. Evaluate @eq-response-xx-drude at filling $\nu\neq1/2$ in an infinite-temperature
   ensemble with a chemical-potential multiplier.
5. A current correlator per unit length behaves as $A t^{-2/3}$ over an
   increasing window. Determine the apparent time-dependent diffusion constant
   and explain why fitting a constant dc conductivity is premature.
6. Design a boundary-driven numerical study that distinguishes a contact
   resistance from a size-dependent bulk resistance. Specify bias, size, and
   convergence checks.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution: filling-dependent free current"}
For independent momentum modes with occupation $\nu$,
$\operatorname{Var}n_k=\nu(1-\nu)$. Hence
$\langle J^2\rangle/L=J^2\nu(1-\nu)/2$ and
$T\mathcal D=J^2\nu(1-\nu)/4$. The result vanishes in the empty/full limits,
where no charge can be transported, and reduces to $J^2/16$ at half filling.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution sketch: a divergent current integral"}
The cutoff Green–Kubo integral is proportional to
$\int^t ds\,s^{-2/3}\sim3t^{1/3}$. If the static susceptibility is finite,
$D(t)\propto t^{1/3}$ and the density variance grows as
$2\int^t ds\,D(s)\propto t^{4/3}$. The spreading distance scales as $t^{2/3}$,
corresponding to dynamical exponent $z=3/2$. This inference uses the stated
window and does not establish the exact asymptotic scaling function.
:::
